response.query: What minimum detectable effect (MDE) can we detect given observed pre-treatment MTL variance, clustering, and staggered adoption, and which subgroup/sample sizes are feasible?
response.answer: The minimum detectable effect (MDE) depends on sample size, significance level, and statistical power; it's the smallest effect reliably detectable given these factors. Larger sample sizes reduce MDE, allowing detection of smaller effects. MDE helps determine feasible subgroup/sample sizes for reliable results.

results.title: Minimum Detectable Effect (MDE) Calculator | MetricGate
results.content: The minimum detectable effect (MDE) is the smallest true difference between a treatment and a control group that an experiment can reliably detect given its sample size, significance level, and statistical power. It is the complement of sample size calculation: rather than asking how many observations you need to detect a given effect, MDE asks what effect size you can detect with the observations you have. If your MDE is 5 percentage points but you only expect a 1 percentage-point lift, launching the experiment would waste resources — you would be highly unlikely to see statistical significance even if the effect is real. For a two-proportion z-test, the MDE is derived from the sample size formula by solving for the effect size: *MDE ≈ (z\_(1−α/2) + z\_(1−β)) · √(2 · p̄ · (1 − p̄) / n)*, where *p̄* is the baseline conversion rate, *n* is the sample size per group, and the z-scores correspond to the chosen significance level and power.

results.title: Understanding Minimum Detectable Effect in AB Testing
results.content: The Minimum Detectable Effect (MDE) is the smallest true effect an A/B test can detect with sufficient statistical power, factoring in test duration, sample size and practical significance. ## What Is MDE? Minimum detectable effect (MDE) is pretty simple on the surface, but it’s also one of the most confusing and misunderstood terms in online A/B testing. 💡 **The most common misunderstanding** is that the MDE is the smallest lift in an A/B test that will be statistically significant. That’s what MDE is!”. ***The answer is that the MDE is about the true effect, whereas the result you get from the test is the observed effect.***. *(Note: For simplicity, we’re using one-tailed tests in this article, which is also what you should use in almost all A/B testing scenarios, but that’s a topic for another time).*. It’s the answer to the question: “If the variant is actually better, and we want, at minimum, an 80% chance of confirming that with our test, how much better does the variant need to be?”.

results.title: What is Minimum Detectable Effect in A/B Testing?
results.content: # Minimum Detectable Effect. The Minimum Detectable Effect (MDE) is a crucial concept in experiment design and A/B testing. * Minimum Detectable Effect helps evaluate whether an experiment result is reliable enough to act on. ## What Minimum Detectable Effect means in A/B testing. In an A/B testing workflow, Minimum Detectable Effect is part of the statistical layer that helps explain whether a result is trustworthy. It is most useful when paired with a clear hypothesis, a primary metric, enough traffic, and a pre-defined decision rule. Grasping the concept of MDE is crucial for several reasons: Experiment Design : It helps you determine the appropriate sample size and duration for your experiments. ## How to use Minimum Detectable Effect. Use Minimum Detectable Effect after you have chosen a primary metric and collected enough traffic for a reliable read. A common mistake is treating Minimum Detectable Effect as a yes-or-no shortcut while ignoring sample size, test duration, and practical business impact.

results.title: Minimum Detectable Effect (MDE) • SplitMetrics
results.content: # Minimum Detectable Effect (MDE). It’s a minimum improvement over the conversion rate of the existing asset (baseline conversion rate) that you want the experiment to detect. By setting MDE, you define the conversion rate increase sufficient for the system to declare the new asset a winner. The lower the MDE is, the more traffic you need to detect minor changes, hence the more money you have to spend on driving that traffic. **Minimum detectable effect is a crucial parameter for evaluating the cost and potential return on running A/B experiments.** From the practical perspective of mobile app marketers, choosing the appropriate value of MDE means striking the balance between the cost of acquiring paid traffic for an experiment and achieving meaningful return on investment. ***To put it in the most practical terms for*** ***SplitMetrics Optimize*** ***users:*** *by setting a lower target MDE, you’re instructing the system to collect more views of your app’s product pages before marking the test as statistically significant and completing it.*.

results.title: Power, Effect Sizes, and Minimum Detectable Effects
results.content: Power is sometimes also called “sensitivity.” Power refers to the ability of a test (i.e., an analysis of an experiment) to detect a “true effect” that is different from the null hypothesis (e.g., the ability to detect a difference between treatment and control when that difference actually exists). There are four factors that influence power: sample size, the true effect size, the variance of the effect, and the alpha-threshold (level of significance). If we have a more liberal threshold (i.e., a higher alpha level), we have more power to detect the effect. But this higher power is due to the fact that the more liberal treshold also increases our “false positive” rate, where the analysis is more likely to say there is an effect when in fact there is not. MDE tell us what is the smallest true effect, in standard deviations of the outcome, that is detectable for a given level of power and statistical significance.
